pinboard.title: Mayberry — The Public's Library System
Masullo on the Riemann Hypothesis
pinboard.description:
Masullo on the Riemann Hypothesis
Posted by John Baez

On November 20, 2026, two attempts to prove the Riemann Hypothesis appeared. One, by Levent Alpöge working with Claude, exists mainly as 17 million lines of Lean code. The other, by Alessandro Masullo, is a 940-page human-written manuscript that Ravi Vakil posted on his blog:

• Ravi Vakil, Hurried announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH, Math 216 blog, November 20, 2026.

• Alessandro Maria Masullo, The Music of the Primes, draft, November 20, 2026.

While there’s been an enormous outpouring about the drama of this situation, so far it’s hard to find good simple accounts of Masullo’s paper. Let me try to fill this gap by sketching Masullo’s proof strategy in a very simplified way, along with some problems people have noted.

Since I am not an expert on number theory, all this is very tentative and I could be making serious mistakes. Please let me know if you see some!

If you also want a sketch of the Alpöge / Claude attempt, check out these:

• Michael Rubinstein, The Alpöge-Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis explained for the Riemann zeta function.

• Jimmie Adriazola, An end-to-end reconstruction of the Alpöge–Claude route to the Riemann hypothesis.
Zeros as poles

Okay—here we go! The Riemann zeta function is

\displaystyle{ \zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^s} = \prod_p \frac{1}{1 - p^{-s}} }

pinboard.title: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button • Ars Technica
pinboard.description:
Ryan Whitwam:

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search. The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”

Remarkably, the "I'm Feeling Lucky" button is still there. It's never been clear whether it gives you the top result, or one that it randomly chooses. Might be too late to find out now?
